Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e111.summary: Opening fragment of the literal exposition of the Lombard's prologue, quoting its incipit ('Cupientes') and beginning the sentence that the Master prefixes a prologue to the work (continued in the next paragraph).

Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e122.summary: States the purpose and structure of the Lombard's prologue: to draw hearers and readers to love the work, the Master commends it in three ways — by the dignity of its subject matter, the rationality of its mode of proceeding, and the fruit and utility it yields — paralleling the threefold commendation of the science of the soul at the beginning of Aristotle's De anima (dignity of subject, certitude, utility).
claims: The Lombard's prologue commends the Sentences by its matter's dignity, its rational method, and its utility.
This threefold commendation mirrors Aristotle's commendation of the science of the soul in De anima 1.

Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e153.summary: Divides the prologue into three parts (dignity of matter; rationality of method, beginning 'Horum igitur'; utility, beginning 'Non igitur debet hic labor') and explains three ways of showing the dignity of a work's matter: from our deficiency before it (our intellect is to the most manifest things as the owl's eye to daylight), from its arduousness and remoteness from sense (as metaphysics is noblest for being most abstract, Metaph. 6), and from the backbiting of the envious (the more hidden a matter, the more easily men lie about it, Ethics 4). Since each of these is a deterrent (retractivum), the Lombard pairs each with an incentive (incitativum): desire to progress, the reward promised by Christ, and the progress of the brethren. Giles then expounds 'aliquid de penuria ac tenuitate nostra' as a threefold humility — of talent ('aliquid'), of practice in eloquence ('penuria', concerning exterior things), and of learning ('tenuitas', concerning interior things) — and explains the widow's mite cast into the gazophylacium (Luke 21), etymologized as a treasury of riches, as Sacred Scripture, where the spiritual riches of reasons defending it are deposited.
claims: The prologue has three parts: dignity of matter, rationality of method, and utility.
A matter's dignity can be shown from our weakness before it, its arduousness, and the detraction it attracts.
The Lombard pairs each deterrent (retractivum) to writing with a corresponding incentive (incitativum).
The Lombard's 'penuria ac tenuitas' expresses humility about his talent, eloquence, and learning.
The gazophylacium of the Lord signifies Sacred Scripture as a treasury of reasons defending it.

Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e288.summary: Expounds the second ground of the work's dignity, the arduousness of its matter ('ardua scandere'), divided into the deterrent, the incentive ('consummationis fiduciam'), and the comparison of the two ('delectant nos'). 'Scaling the arduous' means ascending to divine things, which are lofty and reached by degrees: leaving sensibles (surpassing natural science), passing beyond what is in sensibles (surpassing mathematics), transcending what has sensibles as part of its subject (placing theology above metaphysics), and then beholding divine things — or alternatively ascending through sense, imagination, and natural reason. The Lombard presumed a work beyond his powers, which would fail without divine aid; against this deterrent he sets his trust in the reward from the Good Samaritan (sentence continues).
claims: 'Ardua scandere' signifies ascent to divine things by degrees.
Theology lies above natural science, mathematics, and metaphysics in the order of abstraction from sense.
Undertaking theology exceeds human powers without divine aid.

Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e350.summary: Allegorizes the Good Samaritan as the Lombard's incentive: the Samaritan is Christ; the half-dead man is humanity, stripped of gratuitous gifts and wounded in natural ones by sin; the two denarii are the two Testaments; the works of supererogation are expositions of the two Testaments, such as the Lombard composed, for which he hoped Christ's promised repayment. Giles then begins the comparison of deterrents and incentives ('delectat nos'), showing first how they are set against each other and then that the incentives, through zeal, prevail (continued).
claims: In the parable, Christ is the Samaritan, sinful humanity the half-dead man, and the two Testaments the two denarii.
Expositions of Scripture like the Sentences are works of supererogation that merit reward from Christ.
Sin despoils humanity of gratuitous gifts and wounds its natural ones.

Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e389.summary: Continues the exposition (opening with a garbled transcription): the immensity of labor and weakness deter, the delight of truth and desire to progress encourage, and zeal for God's house — intense love for the Church — wins out, inflaming the Lombard to fortify the faith against carnal men (erring through bodily pleasure) and animal men (erring through depraved intellect) with the 'shields of David's tower', i.e. the reasons of Scripture or of the Church, or rather to show it already fortified by the saints' reasons; to open the hidden matters of theological inquiry (Books 1–3) and to impart knowledge of the sacraments (Book 4). Giles then turns to the third ground of dignity, the detraction of the envious: the 'bigae' of tongue and pen, driven by Christ's charity, are the chariot by which Scripture passes from master to disciple (from Augustine, De Trinitate 3); every human speech is exposed to calumny; its intrinsic cause is that malice in the affect breeds blindness in the intellect, so that truth either goes unseen or offends those whose bad will it rebukes; its extrinsic cause is the devil, 'god of this age', working in the sons of distrust (Ephesians 2). He finally announces the threefold treatment of how such detractors fail to attain truth.
claims: The Lombard's incentives — zeal and love for the Church — overcome the deterrents of weakness and labor.
The Sentences defend faith against carnal and animal errors by showing it fortified by the reasons of the saints.
Books 1–3 of the Sentences open theological questions, Book 4 treats the sacraments.
Malice in the affect produces blindness in the intellect.
Detraction has an intrinsic cause (disordered will) and an extrinsic cause (the devil).
concepts: malitia in affectu, caecitas in intellectu

Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e564.summary: Gives three causes why someone fails to attain truth — not subjecting the will to reason (impeding discovery), not applying study to doctrine (impeding learning), and trying to make things conform to one's mind rather than the mind to things — and then expounds how detractors depart from the threefold way of those who follow truth: they reason for what pleases rather than for truth, and to defend a position rather than to understand (continued).
claims: Truth is missed by not subjecting will to reason, by neglecting study, and by conforming things to the mind rather than the mind to things.
Followers of truth reason for truth's sake and in order to understand, not to defend a position or please.

Gi9qrR-de8172-d1e606.summary: Completes the exposition of the prologue. The third mark of truth-seekers is to be taught according to truth, not turned to fables, and the Lombard sums up detractors as seeking what pleases, not desiring what should be taught, and fitting doctrine to their desires. Their falsity is threefold (falsity being inadequation): surface discordant with depth (superstition, hypocrisy), words discordant with conscience, and words discordant with each other; they corrupt the holiness of faith, tickle the ears of hearers with novelties, and wage contentious war against truth. Turning to the second part ('Horum igitur'), Giles shows the work's rationality by its four causes: final (to stop the mouths of those who make the Church hateful, and to set the lamp of truth on its stand), efficient (God principally, the Lombard instrumentally), material (testimonies of truth founded forever), and formal — both the form of the treatise (four books) and the mode of treating, which sets forth examples, refutes heretics' 'viperine' doctrine, opens access to truth, avoids error by a middle course between Arius and Sabellius, and adheres to the Fathers' limits. The third part ('Non igitur debet') shows the work's utility from its brevity, its firmness (confirmed by patristic testimony), its depth (inviting a free corrector who corrects for correction's sake, not envy), and its orderliness.
claims: Falsity, as inadequation, appears as discord of surface and depth, words and conscience, and words with one another.
The Sentences' rationality is shown through its four causes, with God as principal and the Lombard as instrumental efficient cause.
The Lombard's method steers between Arius's division of substance and Sabellius's confusion of persons.
The work's utility lies in its brevity, patristic firmness, depth, and order.
A true corrector corrects freely for the sake of correction, not out of envy.

Gi9qrR-de8172.summary: Giles's literal exposition (divisio textus) of Peter Lombard's prologue to the Sentences reads it as a threefold commendation modeled on Aristotle's De anima: the dignity of the work's matter, its rational method, and its utility. Dignity is shown by three deterrents, each paired with an incentive — the author's humble weakness (with his desire to progress, and the widow's mite cast into Scripture's treasury), the arduous ascent to divine things beyond natural science, mathematics, and metaphysics (with the reward promised by Christ the Good Samaritan for expositions of the two Testaments), and the detraction of the envious (with the requests of the brethren and the zeal of charity) — the incentives prevailing. Giles analyzes detraction's causes (malice blinding the intellect; the devil), the ways detractors miss truth, and their threefold falsity. The work's rationality is shown through its four causes (to refute error and illuminate truth; God and the Lombard; patristic testimony; four books and a mode of treatment steering between Arius and Sabellius), and its utility through its brevity, firmness, depth, and order.
claims: The Lombard's prologue commends the Sentences by the dignity of its matter, the rationality of its method, and its utility.
Each deterrent to undertaking the work is overcome by a corresponding incentive rooted in charity.
The Sentences is rational because it proceeds through all four causes.
Opposition to truth arises from disordered will and diabolical influence.
